# Supermatter Engine The supermatter engine is an incredibly dangerous, volatile, and radioactive source of power. Without careful management, the supermatter chamber will fill with fire, hypercharged lightning will arc out, and, eventually, an explosion will obliterate everything.
With proper care and handling, the supermatter can be an incredibly potent power source for the station. The crystal absorbs a sample of the chamber gas, processes it, and returns most of it; only reactive gases such as ammonia/miasma are consumed. The mix's heat capacity, heat resistance, heat-to-power ratio, and lightning power transmission all matter a great deal. Once the crystal is running, tesla coils harvest its lightning arcs for the grid.
## Precautions
[bold][color=red]DO NOT INTENTIONALLY ACTIVATE THE CRYSTAL BEFORE COOLING HAS BEEN SET UP.[/color][/bold]
Before stepping into the supermatter chamber, there are a few things to keep in mind to avert disaster and personal harm.
• Do not power the crystal before the cooling loop has been set up. [color=red]Do not touch the crystal. Do not walk into the crystal.[/color]
• Keep clear of the crystal's lightning arcs. Insulated gloves and grounding rods are your protection; the arcs will happily strike people and machinery.
• Wear radiation protection around the crystal at all times. Supermatter radiation is a hazard, not a power source.
• Do not stare directly into the crystal. Its light is intense and its arcs are unpredictable.
• If you must approach the crystal, equip and enable magboots.
• A delamination at high internal energy can level a very large area. See the warning at the end of this entry.
## Supermatter Crystal
The supermatter crystal is the main focus of the supermatter engine. It absorbs a sample of the gas around it, uses the gas as a coolant and working fluid, and emits both radiation and lightning.
When powered — usually by emitters — the intensity of its arcs and radiation will grow, as hot oxygen and plasma are released as waste. To top it all off, [color=red]anything that touches the crystal is instantly vaporized, including you[/color].
## Radiation
The crystal is radioactive. This radiation is a hazard only: it damages crew and grows worse as the crystal loses integrity, but it will never charge a radiation collector. Radiation collectors are not part of this engine; keep them out of the chamber and rely on tesla coils for power. Wear radiation protection and keep the crystal's integrity high.
## Tesla Coils
Tesla coils are the crystal's power path. Place them near the chamber, connect them to HV cables, and the crystal will arc directly into them. Each strike charges the coil's internal battery, which then discharges into the grid.
The crystal supports the nearest one coil at base power and one more for every 4,000 points of effective power. It only re-strikes a coil after that coil has discharged, so a coil's output follows the grid's actual draw. Extra coils beyond that supported set are not charged. Gas composition modifies effective power through its power transmission: plasma and tritium amplify it, while freon and water vapor suppress it. Grounding rods protect nearby areas from the incidental arcs.
Coils and grounding rods take lightning damage and will require regular welding to prevent them from being destroyed. Ensure they are placed in strategic yet accessible locations.
The amount, strength, and range of the lightning emissions will increase along with how much energy the crystal contains. Be prepared to deal with the extra arcs if you run a high-power setup. The crystal's main power discharge feeds tesla coils; its incidental arcs use SS13's priority for grounding rods, crew, machinery, and loose objects.
## Cooling Loop
At the most fundamental level, the supermatter crystal is kept stable with a "loop" of atmospheric pipes. The chamber is filled with safe, cold gas, and the loop carries the reaction heat away. Most of the gas is returned after processing, but reactive gases such as ammonia/miasma are consumed and any harmful byproducts should be filtered out of the system.
Most stations will come with pre-supplied nitrogen canisters: nitrogen is stable and easy to keep cool, which makes it an ideal coolant for a basic setup.
To set up the cooling loop, anchor the nitrogen canisters to the input connector ports and enable the respective gas pumps. Follow the pipes, enabling gas pumps and filters as you go.
Be careful not to activate the gas pumps inside the interior chamber's airlocks before the full cooling loop is set up. A bypass gas pump is located outside the external airlock; use this to keep gas flowing as you work.
At least one of the filters that feeds back into the loop should be set to filter nitrogen. This will keep the cooled nitrogen in the loop, ensuring the crystal is kept at safe parameters. If you deliberately run a different coolant mix, return those gases instead, or the loop will slowly drain the mix.
Once the full cooling loop has been set up, check with a gas analyzer to make sure the gas is not trapped at any point in the system. Disable the bypass gas pump by the airlocks, enable the interior gas pumps, and configure the air alarm.
## Air Alarm Configuration
Ensure you have an air alarm connected to the devices in the chamber.
By default, the air vents in the supermatter's chamber will only output up to 101.3 kPa of gas, and adhere to pressure lockout parameters.
Using the air alarm, increase the output threshold of each vent, or switch them to internal pressure bounds. The pressure lockout features of each vent should also be disabled.
The air scrubbers also need adjustment from their default configuration. Ensure each scrubber is set to filter the waste gases you actually need to remove, and that the WideNet feature is enabled for maximum efficiency. If you set a chamber scrubber to filter all gases, its output must pass through the loop filter that returns your coolant; otherwise the scrubber will strip the coolant out of the chamber. If you use a CO2/O2 mix instead of nitrogen, configure the loop filter to return those gases as well.
## Emitters
Once the cooling loop is fully set up and the tesla coils are wired to the grid, the supermatter engine is ready to start up.
Emitters are the most common way of kickstarting the supermatter and keeping its internal energy high. Interact with an emitter to toggle it on, and it will begin firing lasers at the crystal.
## Experimentation
Although nitrogen is good at keeping the supermatter safe and stable, it also lowers the crystal's heat-to-power transfer and lightning transmission. Reactive gases such as ammonia/miasma are consumed, so keep an eye on the mix.
The supermatter monitoring console allows close observation of the crystal, its tesla coil output, and the effects that gases have on it. This is a key piece of equipment for safely experimenting with the supermatter.
Carbon dioxide is excellent at amplifying the supermatter's internal energy, while nitrous oxide can improve the supermatter's heat tolerance. Be careful: a CO2-rich mix can suppress power decay almost entirely. If the crystal has no way to shed power, it will run away; keep the mix balanced and watch the console.
## Safe Operation
For a first engine, use a supermatter shard with nitrogen coolant, keep internal energy around 1,500–2,000, use one tesla coil, at least two grounding rods, radiation shutters, and a monitoring console. That produces about 350 kW and a 7-tile failure radius. Do not add plasma, tritium, or a CO2-rich mix until the cooling loop is proven and someone is watching the console.
## Delamination
If the crystal is destroyed, it detonates instead of leaving a singularity or a tesla ball behind. The blast starts at 20 tiles and grows by one tile for every 4,000 points of internal energy it is holding when it fails. The shard uses a much smaller blast, matching its SS13 counterpart. The 60-second countdown can still be averted if the crystal's integrity recovers above the delamination point before it expires.
Delamination also scatters 1–6 hyperflux anomalies based on how much energy the crystal held. At low energy a single anomaly appears; at maximum severity six are released. Hyperflux anomalies are ordinary science anomalies: they can be scanned, stabilized with the correct particles, or contained in an anomaly vessel like any other anomaly. A high-energy failure can therefore level far more than the chamber. Keep the crystal cool, keep its power controlled, and do not let it reach the delamination point.
